claim: Telomeres are composed of TTAGGG repeats in mammals.
source: These capping structures have the crucial function of maintaining genome stability by protecting the chromosome end from being recognised as DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) (Palm and de Lange, 2008). They also represent challenging structures for the replication machinery, which is associated to telomere fragile sites (Martínez et al., 2009; McNees et al., 2010; Sfeir et al., 2009; Vannier et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Moyzis et al., 1988, which is a reference to published work.

claim: Telomeres are composed of six associated proteins that form the shelterin complex: TRF1, TRF2, POT1a/b, RAP1 and TIN2.
source: Telomeres are specialised nucleoprotein structures at the ends of chromosomes, composed of repetitive sequences (TTAGGG repeats in mammals) (Moyzis et al., 1988), long non-coding RNA called TERRA and six associated proteins, TRF1, TRF2, POT1a/b, RAP1 and TIN2, that form the shelterin complex (de Lange, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to de Lange, 2005.

claim: Telomeres have the crucial function of maintaining genome stability by protecting chromosome ends from being recognised as DNA double strand breaks.
source: These capping structures have the crucial function of maintaining genome stability by protecting the chromosome end from being recognised as DNA double strand breaks (DSBs) (Palm and de Lange, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Palm and de Lange, 2008.

claim: Telomeres represent challenging structures for the replication machinery, which is associated with telomere fragile sites.
source: They also represent challenging structures for the replication machinery, which is associated to telomere fragile sites (Martínez et al., 2009; McNees et al., 2010; Sfeir et al., 2009; Vannier et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: Telomere fragility is identified by the formation of multitelomeric signals (MTS), where telomeres appear as broken or decondensed.
source: Telomere fragility is identified by the formation of multitelomeric signals (MTS), where telomeres appear as broken or decondensed, resembling the common fragile sites (CFS) observed at non telomeric loci after treatment with aphidicolin (APH).
evidence: The claim is a direct statement from the text defining telomere fragility.

claim: TRF1 facilitates the progression of the replication fork at telomeres by recruiting the DNA helicase BLM.
source: TRF1 facilitates the progression of the replication fork at telomeres, by recruiting a specialised DNA helicase BLM, which in turn resolve secondary structures, similar to fission yeast ortholog Taz1 (Lee et al., 2018; Martínez et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2006; Sfeir et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: BLM resolves secondary structures at telomeres.
source: TRF1 facilitates the progression of the replication fork at telomeres, by recruiting a specialised DNA helicase BLM, which in turn resolve secondary structures, similar to fission yeast ortholog Taz1 (Lee et al., 2018; Martínez et al., 2009; Miller et al., 2006; Sfeir et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: The majority of cancer cells reactivate telomerase to achieve replicative immortality.
source: The majority of cancer cells reactivate telomerase, while a minority (10–15%) uses an alternative mechanism named ALT for alternative lengthening of telomeres (Bryan et al., 1997; Kim et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bryan et al., 1997 and Kim et al., 1994.

claim: 10-15% of cancer cells use an alternative mechanism named ALT for alternative lengthening of telomeres.
source: The majority of cancer cells reactivate telomerase, while a minority (10–15%) uses an alternative mechanism named ALT for alternative lengthening of telomeres (Bryan et al., 1997; Kim et al., 1994).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bryan et al., 1997 and Kim et al., 1994.

claim: ALT is characterised by the appearance of ALT-associated PML bodies (APBs).
source: Intriguingly, ALT is characterised by the appearance of ALT-associated PML bodies (APBs), specialised sites where a subset of telomeres co-localises with PML protein and several DNA repair and homologous recombination (HR) proteins (Draskovic et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2000; Yeager et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Draskovic et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2000; Yeager et al., 1999.

claim: APBs are specialised sites where a subset of telomeres co-localises with PML protein and several DNA repair and homologous recombination proteins.
source: Intriguingly, ALT is characterised by the appearance of ALT-associated PML bodies (APBs), specialised sites where a subset of telomeres co-localises with PML protein and several DNA repair and homologous recombination (HR) proteins (Draskovic et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2000; Yeager et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Draskovic et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2000; Yeager et al., 1999.

claim: In yeast, two different ALT-like pathways have been described: type I and type II, both dependent on Rad52.
source: Indeed, in yeast, two different ALT-like pathways have been described: type I and type II, both dependent on Rad52.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement from the text about yeast ALT pathways.

claim: Type I ALT mechanism requires Rad51 to mediate the invasion of a homologous sequence.
source: While Type I requires Rad51 to mediate the invasion of a homologous sequence, Type II is Rad51 independent but Rad50 (of the MRX/N complex) dependent.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement from the text describing Type I ALT mechanism.

claim: Type II ALT mechanism is Rad51 independent but Rad50 (of the MRX/N complex) dependent.
source: While Type I requires Rad51 to mediate the invasion of a homologous sequence, Type II is Rad51 independent but Rad50 (of the MRX/N complex) dependent.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement from the text describing Type II ALT mechanism.

claim: Both Type I and II ALT mechanisms require the DNA polymerase Pol32, which initiates DNA synthesis for several kilobases in a process known as Break Induced Replication (BIR).
source: Both Type I and II mechanisms require the DNA polymerase Pol32, which initiates DNA synthesis for several kilobases, in a process known as Break Induced Replication (BIR) (Ira and Haber, 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ira and Haber, 2002.

claim: Mammalian BIR is dependent on POLD3 and POLD4, subunits of DNA polymerase delta and orthologs of yeast Pol32.
source: Recently, multiple groups have revisited this Rad51 independent DNA synthesis repair pathway at mammalian ALT telomeres (Dilley et al., 2016; Garcia-Exposito et al., 2016; Roumelioti et al., 2016). Mammalian BIR is dependent on POLD3 and POLD4, subunits of DNA polymerase delta and orthologs of yeast Pol32.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement from the text about mammalian BIR, with citations to Dilley et al., 2016; Garcia-Exposito et al., 2016; Roumelioti et al., 2016.

claim: ALT cells present increased DNA damage response.
source: ALT cells present increased DNA damage response (DDR) and several studies have underlined the contribution of replication stress to ALT-mediated telomere extension (Arora et al., 2014; Cox et al., 2016; Pan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Arora et al., 2014; Cox et al., 2016; Pan et al., 2017.

claim: Replication stress contributes to ALT-mediated telomere extension.
source: ALT cells present increased DNA damage response (DDR) and several studies have underlined the contribution of replication stress to ALT-mediated telomere extension (Arora et al., 2014; Cox et al., 2016; Pan et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Arora et al., 2014; Cox et al., 2016; Pan et al., 2017.

claim: Telomeres lacking TRF1 are enriched in SMC5/6, DNA polymerase δ (POLD3), and chromatin remodelling factors known to be associated with ALT telomeres.
source: Surprisingly, we found that telomeres lacking TRF1 are enriched in SMC5/6, DNA polymerase δ (POLD3), and chromatin remodelling factors known to be associated with ALT telomeres.
evidence: The claim is based on the PICh experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TRF1 deleted cells present additional DNA damage and recombination hallmarks such as formation of APBs.
source: These cells also present additional DNA damage and recombination hallmarks such as formation of APBs, mitotic DNA synthesis at telomeres, a feature of BIR and increased TERRA levels.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TRF1 deleted cells present mitotic DNA synthesis at telomeres, a feature of BIR.
source: These cells also present additional DNA damage and recombination hallmarks such as formation of APBs, mitotic DNA synthesis at telomeres, a feature of BIR and increased TERRA levels.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TRF1 deleted cells present increased TERRA levels.
source: These cells also present additional DNA damage and recombination hallmarks such as formation of APBs, mitotic DNA synthesis at telomeres, a feature of BIR and increased TERRA levels.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: SMC5/6 complex and POLD3 are key regulators of the recombination signature identified in TRF1 deleted cells.
source: Further investigation using specific shRNAs against the SMC5/6 complex or POLD3 revealed how these two complexes are key regulators of the recombination signature identified in TRF1 deleted cells.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data using shRNAs presented in the manuscript.

claim: TRF1 is a central player in preserving telomeric chromatin against HR induced by DNA replication stress.
source: Taken together, these results strongly identify TRF1 as a central player in preserving telomeric chromatin against HR, induced by DNA replication stress, and particularly POLD3 dependent-mitotic DNA synthesis.
evidence: The claim is based on the collective interpretation of experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TRF1 is a central player in preserving telomeric chromatin against POLD3 dependent-mitotic DNA synthesis.
source: Taken together, these results strongly identify TRF1 as a central player in preserving telomeric chromatin against HR, induced by DNA replication stress, and particularly POLD3 dependent-mitotic DNA synthesis.
evidence: The claim is based on the collective interpretation of experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: MEFs lacking TRF1 can grow for up to 8 days before entering senescence.
source: MEFs lacking TRF1 are well known to undergo replicative stress; however, they can grow for up to 8 days before entering senescence, making them optimal for investigating replication stress at telomeres (Martínez et al., 2009; Sfeir et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Martínez et al., 2009; Sfeir et al., 2009.

claim: Excision of exon 1 of TRF1 by CRE recombinase resulted in the loss of TRF1 protein.
source: Excision of exon 1 of TRF1 by CRE recombinase (Sfeir et al., 2009) resulted in the expected loss of TRF1 protein as determined by immunoblotting and deficient cells do not show drastic change in the cell cycle distribution (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by immunoblotting data shown in Figure 1B and referenced in the text.

claim: TRF1 deficient cells do not show drastic change in the cell cycle distribution.
source: Excision of exon 1 of TRF1 by CRE recombinase (Sfeir et al., 2009) resulted in the expected loss of TRF1 protein as determined by immunoblotting and deficient cells do not show drastic change in the cell cycle distribution (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 119 proteins presented a gain of abundance at TRF1 depleted telomeres.
source: Based on the analysis of label free quantification (LFQ intensities), we found 119 proteins presenting a gain of abundance at TRF1 depleted telomeres (Log2<-2) and 206 factors were displaced from these telomeres (Log2>-2), considering that a cut-off for differential expression is set to log2 fold change (TRF1deletion/wt)> |2| and -Log (p-value) > 1 (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is based on mass spectrometry data analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: 206 factors were displaced from TRF1 depleted telomeres.
source: Based on the analysis of label free quantification (LFQ intensities), we found 119 proteins presenting a gain of abundance at TRF1 depleted telomeres (Log2<-2) and 206 factors were displaced from these telomeres (Log2>-2), considering that a cut-off for differential expression is set to log2 fold change (TRF1deletion/wt)> |2| and -Log (p-value) > 1 (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is based on mass spectrometry data analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: CTC1, a component of the CST complex, is less abundant at TRF1 depleted telomeres.
source: Amongst these 206 proteins, we found TRF1, as expected due to the knock-out of its gene, but also one component of the CST complex (CTC1), important player in the efficient restart of stalled replication forks at telomeres (Gu et al., 2012) and recruited through POT1b interaction (Wu et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is based on PICh mass spectrometry data, with citations to Gu et al., 2012 and Wu et al., 2012 for CTC1 function.

claim: POT1b is less abundant at TRF1 depleted telomeres.
source: Interestingly, POT1b is also less abundant at TRF1 depleted telomeres (Figure 1D–E).
evidence: The claim is based on PICh mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1D-E.

claim: The group of 119 proteins enriched in TRF1 deleted cells includes several factors involved in structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC), HR and DNA damage response.
source: On the other end, the group of 119 proteins enriched in TRF1 deleted cells includes several factors involved in structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC), HR and DNA damage response (Figure 1D–E–F), such as the MRN complex (MRE11, RAD50 and NBS1).
evidence: The claim is based on PICh mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1D-E-F.

claim: The MRN complex (MRE11, RAD50 and NBS1) is enriched at TRF1 depleted telomeres.
source: On the other end, the group of 119 proteins enriched in TRF1 deleted cells includes several factors involved in structural maintenance of chromosomes (SMC), HR and DNA damage response (Figure 1D–E–F), such as the MRN complex (MRE11, RAD50 and NBS1).
evidence: The claim is based on PICh mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1D-E-F.

claim: 53BP1 is recruited to TRF1 depleted telomeres.
source: The identification of 53BP1 recruited to TRF1 depleted telomeres (Figure 1D–F) acts as a positive marker for the specificity of this proteomic analysis, as reported before in Martínez et al. (2009); Sfeir et al. (2009).
evidence: The claim is based on PICh mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 1D-F, with citations to Martínez et al. (2009); Sfeir et al. (2009).

claim: TRF1 deficient MEFs present a telomeric enrichment for factors involved in HR and chromatin remodelling (BRCA1, PML, SMC5/6, ATRX and, NurD associated factors) that are usually abundant at ALT telomeres.
source: Interestingly, TRF1 deficient MEFs present a telomeric enrichment for factors involved in HR and chromatin remodelling (BRCA1, PML, SMC5/6, ATRX and, NurD associated factors) that are usually abundant at ALT telomeres (Figure 2A) (Conomos et al., 2014; Draskovic et al., 2009; Marzec et al., 2015; Potts and Yu, 2007).
evidence: The claim is based on PICh data shown in Figure 2A, with citations to Conomos et al., 2014; Draskovic et al., 2009; Marzec et al., 2015; Potts and Yu, 2007.

claim: ChIP experiments confirmed the recruitment of BAZ1b, BRCA1 and some subunits of the NurD complex (MTA1, ZNF827 and CHD4) at TRF1 depleted telomeres.
source: TRF1 antibody was used as a negative control for our experiment, while the recruitment of BAZ1b, BRCA1 and some subunits of the nucleosome remodelling and deacetylase (NurD) complex (p66a, MTA1, ZNF827 and CHD4) was assessed. For all these factors, with the exception of p66a for which no statistical significance was achieved, we observed a specific enrichment at telomeres upon TRF1 deletion (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, A).
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-dot blot data shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1, A.

claim: TRF1-/- MEFs show a two-fold increase in the number of co-localisations between PML and telomeres compared to control cells.
source: In addition, to confirm the presence of PML at telomeres lacking TRF1, as suggested by our PICh data (Figure 2A), we performed immuno-FISH and scored for the formation of APBs. We observed a two-fold increase in the number of co-localisations between PML and telomeres in TRF1-/- MEFs compared to control cells (Figure 2C).
evidence: The claim is based on immuno-FISH data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: wt MEFs treated with low doses of APH (0.4 µM) for 3 days did not show recruitment of chromatin remodellers and DNA repair factors BRCA1, MTA1, CHD4, ZNF827 and BAZ1b.
source: To test if the recruitment of some of these factors is a consequence of chronic replication stress or if TRF1 directly inhibit these events, we treated wt MEFs with low doses of APH (0.4 µM) for 3 days. Using ChIP-dot blot, we did not detect the recruitment of any of the chromatin remodellers and DNA repair factors BRCA1, MTA1, CHD4, ZNF827 and BAZ1b, present at TRF1 depleted telomeres (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, B).
evidence: The claim is based on ChIP-dot blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, B.

claim: wt MEFs treated with APH do not form APBs despite a general increase in PML foci.
source: Furthermore, we show that wt MEFs treated with APH do not form APBs despite a general increase in PML foci (Figure 2—figure supplement 1, C).
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1, C.

claim: TRF1-/- MEFs show an increase in T-SCE (2.8%) compared to control cells (0.4%).
source: Hence, to test if TRF1 is a suppressor of recombination, we revisited the incidence of telomeric sister chromatid exchanges (T-SCE) using chromosome orientation FISH (CO-FISH) in TRF1 deficient cells (Figure 2D). We identified an increase in T-SCE in TRF1-/- MEFs (2.8%) compared to control cells (0.4%) (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is based on CO-FISH data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: At day 4 post infection, TRF1-/- cells show 1.6% of T-SCEs per chromosome end.
source: Therefore, we repeated the experiments in TRF1-/- cells at different time points post infection: day 4 and day 7, finding respectively 1.6% and 2.8% of T-SCEs per chromosome end (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, A-left graph), indicating a lower % of T-SCE events happening at earlier time point.
evidence: The claim is based on CO-FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, A.

claim: At day 7 post infection, TRF1-/- cells show 2.8% of T-SCEs per chromosome end.
source: Therefore, we repeated the experiments in TRF1-/- cells at different time points post infection: day 4 and day 7, finding respectively 1.6% and 2.8% of T-SCEs per chromosome end (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, A-left graph), indicating a lower % of T-SCE events happening at earlier time point.
evidence: The claim is based on CO-FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, A.

claim: 4 days post infection, only T-SCEs at single chromatids were significantly increased in TRF1 deficient MEFs.
source: Thus, we next classified T-SCEs detected in TRF1 deficient MEFs into these two different types (single and double) and found that 4 days post infection only T-SCEs at single chromatids were significantly increased (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, A-right graph), while the reciprocal exchanges were not enhanced at TRF1 depleted telomeres (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, A-middle graph).
evidence: The claim is based on CO-FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, A.

claim: Reciprocal exchanges were not enhanced at TRF1 depleted telomeres at 4 days post infection.
source: Thus, we next classified T-SCEs detected in TRF1 deficient MEFs into these two different types (single and double) and found that 4 days post infection only T-SCEs at single chromatids were significantly increased (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, A-right graph), while the reciprocal exchanges were not enhanced at TRF1 depleted telomeres (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, A-middle graph).
evidence: The claim is based on CO-FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, A.

claim: Single chromatid exchanges are characteristic of conservative DNA synthesis – Break Induced Replication.
source: Therefore, our detailed analysis of the nature and timing of T-SCEs in TRF1 deficient MEFs not only demonstrates an unappreciated role of TRF1 in suppressing HR, but also suggests that single chromatid exchanges, characteristic of conservative DNA synthesis – Break Induced Replication (Roumelioti et al., 2016), are the initial events arising in TRF1-/- MEFs.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Roumelioti et al., 2016.

claim: APH-treated MEFs show an increase in single exchanges.
source: To further discriminate between suppression of recombination by TRF1 and replication-dependent recombination, we quantified T-SCEs in mouse cells treated with APH. Like for TRF1-depleted telomeres, we also detected an increase in single exchanges in APH-treated MEFs (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, B-right panel).
evidence: The claim is based on CO-FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, B.

claim: The absence of reciprocal exchanges between telomere chromatids in APH-treated MEFs indicates that APH-dependent replication stress does not trigger an HR repair but only BIR.
source: The absence of reciprocal exchanges between telomere chromatids indicates that APH-dependent replication stress does not trigger an HR repair but only BIR, albeit we cannot completely exclude that longer replication stress could lead to HR (Figure 2—figure supplement 2, B-left panel).
evidence: The claim is based on CO-FISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2, B and inference from the data.

claim: TRF1 has a specific function in suppressing chromatin remodeling, APBs and HR.
source: Overall our data highlights the specific function of TRF1 in suppressing chromatin remodeling, APBs and HR.
evidence: The claim is based on the collective interpretation of experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Previous studies have reported in-vivo interactions between TRF1 and TERRA.
source: Previous studies have reported in-vivo interactions between TRF1 and TERRA (Deng et al., 2009) and also a possible transcriptional regulation by TRF1 through a mechanism involving RNA polymerase II - TRF1 interaction (Schoeftner and Blasco, 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Deng et al., 2009 and Schoeftner and Blasco, 2008.

claim: RNA dot-blot and Northern-blot analyses show a significant increase in TERRA molecules upon loss of TRF1 in immortalised MEFs, 7 days after transduction.
source: We performed both RNA dot-blot and Northern-blot analyses showing a significant increase in TERRA molecules upon loss of TRF1 in immortalised MEFs, 7 days after transduction (Figure 3A–B) but also at earlier time point (day 4) and in primary MEFs (Figure 3—figure supplements 1, A–B–C).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA dot-blot and Northern-blot data shown in Figure 3A-B.

claim: TERRA increase is observed at day 4 post infection in TRF1 deleted cells.
source: We performed both RNA dot-blot and Northern-blot analyses showing a significant increase in TERRA molecules upon loss of TRF1 in immortalised MEFs, 7 days after transduction (Figure 3A–B) but also at earlier time point (day 4) and in primary MEFs (Figure 3—figure supplements 1, A–B–C).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA dot-blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1, A–B–C.

claim: TERRA increase is observed in primary MEFs upon TRF1 deletion.
source: We performed both RNA dot-blot and Northern-blot analyses showing a significant increase in TERRA molecules upon loss of TRF1 in immortalised MEFs, 7 days after transduction (Figure 3A–B) but also at earlier time point (day 4) and in primary MEFs (Figure 3—figure supplements 1, A–B–C).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA dot-blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 1, A–B–C.

claim: TERRAs in TRF1 deficient cells have high molecular weight and can only be detected when an alkaline treatment is performed during Northern-blotting.
source: Particularly, we noticed that these TERRAs have high molecular weight and can only be detected when an alkaline treatment is performed during Northern-blotting (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, D).
evidence: The claim is based on Northern-blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, D.

claim: TERRA-FISH in MEFs deficient for TRF1 shows a significant increase in numbers and intensity of TERRA foci per nucleus.
source: In addition, we carried out TERRA-FISH (Figure 3C) in MEFs deficient for TRF1, confirming a significant increase in numbers and intensity of TERRA foci per nucleus (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is based on TERRA-FISH data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: APH-treated MEFs exhibited a significant increase in TERRAs.
source: To determine whether this phenotype is a direct consequence of replication stress, MEFs were treated with low doses of APH and TERRA analysis was carried out by RNA dot-blot and Northern blot. Similar to TRF1 depleted cells, APH-treated MEFs exhibited a significant increase in TERRAs (Figure 3—figure supplement 1, E–F).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA dot-blot and Northern blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1, E–F.

claim: TRF1-dependent replication stress enhances telomere transcription or TERRAs stability.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that TRF1-dependent replication stress enhances telomere transcription or TERRAs stability.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the TERRA data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TRF1 deficient MEFs show no telomere length heterogeneity.
source: However, the absence of telomere heterogeneity, c-circle formation and still presence of telomerase activity (Figure 3—figure supplements 2, A–B–C) also suggest that this ALT-like phenotype is not complete.
evidence: The claim is based on Terminal Restriction Fragments (TRF) blot data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2, A.

claim: TRF1 deficient MEFs show no c-circle formation.
source: However, the absence of telomere heterogeneity, c-circle formation and still presence of telomerase activity (Figure 3—figure supplements 2, A–B–C) also suggest that this ALT-like phenotype is not complete.
evidence: The claim is based on C-circle assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2, C.

claim: TRF1 deficient MEFs still have telomerase activity.
source: However, the absence of telomere heterogeneity, c-circle formation and still presence of telomerase activity (Figure 3—figure supplements 2, A–B–C) also suggest that this ALT-like phenotype is not complete.
evidence: The claim is based on TRAP assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2, B.

claim: TRF1-depleted HT1080-ST cells present a modest but significant increase in APBs formation.
source: To test whether the function of TRF1 in suppressing these ALT-like features is conserved in human cells, we used small RNA interference against TRF1 in HT1080-ST cells (long telomeres), performing all the analysis 6 days post-transfection (Figure 4A). TRF1-depleted HT1080-ST cells present a modest but significant increase in APBs formation (Figure 4B).
evidence: The claim is based on immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: TRF1 depleted HT1080-ST cells show a significant increase in single exchanges.
source: To assess the human TRF1 function in suppressing HR and BIR, we measured sister chromatid exchanges at telomeres in HT1080-ST depleted for TRF1 (Figure 4C). We observed a significant increase in single exchanges (Figure 4C-right panel) however, we could not detect double exchanges in cells transfected with TRF1 siRNA compared to the ctl (Figure 4C-left panel).
evidence: The claim is based on CO-FISH data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: No double exchanges were detected in HT1080-ST cells transfected with TRF1 siRNA compared to the control.
source: To assess the human TRF1 function in suppressing HR and BIR, we measured sister chromatid exchanges at telomeres in HT1080-ST depleted for TRF1 (Figure 4C). We observed a significant increase in single exchanges (Figure 4C-right panel) however, we could not detect double exchanges in cells transfected with TRF1 siRNA compared to the ctl (Figure 4C-left panel).
evidence: The claim is based on CO-FISH data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: No differences in TERRA expression were observed between control and TRF1 depleted HT1080-ST cells.
source: Finally, TERRA expression was analysed by DNA dot blot and no differences were observed between ctr and TRF1 depleted cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, A).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA dot-blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, A.

claim: No significant increase in TERRAs was detected in human TRF1 KO HeLa cells even 15 days after hTRF1 deletion.
source: To evaluate whether long term depletion of TRF1 in human cells would cause any increase in TERRA expression, as observed in TRF1-/- MEFs, we used a doxycycline inducible TRF1 CRISPR/Cas9 HeLa cell line (Figure 4—figure supplement 1, B) (Kim et al., 2017). However, even 15 days after hTRF1 deletion, no significant increase in TERRAs was detected.
evidence: The claim is based on RNA dot-blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1, B.

claim: Human TRF1 KO cells did not show any growing defects after 15 days in culture.
source: Human TRF1 KO cells did not show any growing defects after 15 days in culture, which is remarkably different from TRF1 deficient MEFs that fail to proliferate due to a rapid induction of senescence (Karlseder et al., 2003; Martínez et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is a direct observation from the experiment, with citations to Karlseder et al., 2003; Martínez et al., 2009 for comparison.

claim: TRF1 deficient MEFs fail to proliferate due to a rapid induction of senescence.
source: Human TRF1 KO cells did not show any growing defects after 15 days in culture, which is remarkably different from TRF1 deficient MEFs that fail to proliferate due to a rapid induction of senescence (Karlseder et al., 2003; Martínez et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Karlseder et al., 2003; Martínez et al., 2009.

claim: Both mouse and human TRF1 suppresses telomere fragility and is essential to facilitate DNA replication through telomeric repeats.
source: For both species, TRF1 suppresses telomere fragility and therefore is essential to facilitate DNA replication through telomeric repeats (Lee et al., 2018; Sfeir et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2018; Sfeir et al., 2009.

claim: Like for mouse TRF1, its human homolog is essential to suppress APBs formation and BIR.
source: We now show that like for mouse TRF1, its human homolog is essential to suppress APBs formation and BIR, which is likely responsible for the rescue of stalled/collapsed telomeric forks.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data presented in the manuscript comparing mouse and human TRF1 functions.

claim: TRF1-/- MEFs display elevated BrdU incorporation at telomeres, showing two-times more telomere synthesis compared to control cells.
source: TRF1-/- MEFs display elevated BrdU incorporation at telomeres, showing two-times more telomere synthesis compared to control cells (Figure 5C).
evidence: The claim is based on BrdU immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: CRE induced cells had a significant increase in telomeric mitotic DNA synthesis compared to the GFP control cells.
source: After incubating wt and TRF1 deficient MEFs with 5-ethynyl-2-deoxyuridine (EdU) and colcemid for 1 hr, mitotic cells were collected to analyse EdU incorporation on metaphase chromosomes (Figure 5A). We scored for telomeric and non-telomeric EdU foci (mitotic DNA synthesis) and found that CRE induced cells had a significant increase in telomeric mitotic DNA synthesis compared to the GFP control cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: The claim is based on EdU-FISH data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: 72% of the mitotic DNA synthesis at non-telomeric sites localised to a single chromatid, while the remaining 28% of the signal was present at both chromatids.
source: In fact, 72% of the mitotic DNA synthesis at non-telomeric sites localised to a single chromatid, while the remaining 28% of the signal was present at both chromatids (Figure 5F, upper panel).
evidence: The claim is based on EdU incorporation analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Almost all the EdU co-localisation at telomeres was present at single chromatids (95%).
source: This result is even more striking when EdU signal was restricted to telomeres, with almost all the co-localisation being present at single chromatids (95%).
evidence: The claim is based on EdU incorporation analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: TRF1 is crucial for the suppression of mitotic DNA synthesis mediated by BIR at telomeres.
source: These observations suggest that TRF1 is crucial for the suppression of mitotic DNA synthesis mediated by BIR at telomeres.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the EdU incorporation data presented in the manuscript.

claim: BIR is a recombination dependent process reinitiating DNA replication when one end of a chromosome shares homology with the template DNA, leading to conservative DNA synthesis, which is dependent on RAD52 and POLD3.
source: BIR is a recombination dependent process reinitiating DNA replication when one end of a chromosome shares homology with the template DNA, leading to conservative DNA synthesis, which is dependent on RAD52 and POLD3 (pol32 homolog in yeast) (Bhowmick et al., 2016; Sotiriou et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bhowmick et al., 2016; Sotiriou et al., 2016.

claim: ALT telomeres have been reported to be elongated by BIR, in a POLD3 and SMC5-dependent manner.
source: ALT telomeres have recently been reported to be elongated by BIR, in a POLD3 and SMC5-dependent manner (Dilley et al., 2016; Min et al., 2017; Potts et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dilley et al., 2016; Min et al., 2017; Potts et al., 2006.

claim: The enrichment of DNA synthesis at telomeres in TRF1 deleted cells was suppressed in the double mutant TRF1-POLD3.
source: Thus, we carried out EdU-FISH in these cells to check for the presence of BIR (Figure 6D). We found that the enrichment of DNA synthesis at telomeres in TRF1 deleted cells was suppressed in the double mutant TRF1-POLD3, while the double mutant TRF1-SMC5 revealed similar telomeric DNA synthesis when compared to the single TRF1 mutant (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is based on EdU-FISH data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: The double mutant TRF1-SMC5 revealed similar telomeric DNA synthesis when compared to the single TRF1 mutant.
source: Thus, we carried out EdU-FISH in these cells to check for the presence of BIR (Figure 6D). We found that the enrichment of DNA synthesis at telomeres in TRF1 deleted cells was suppressed in the double mutant TRF1-POLD3, while the double mutant TRF1-SMC5 revealed similar telomeric DNA synthesis when compared to the single TRF1 mutant (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is based on EdU-FISH data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: BIR is the molecular mechanism taking place at TRF1 depleted telomeres.
source: First, these results confirm that BIR is the molecular mechanism taking place at TRF1 depleted telomeres.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the EdU-FISH data in double mutants.

claim: SMC5 appears to be dispensable for BIR dependent DNA synthesis at TRF1 depleted telomeres.
source: Second, SMC5 appears to be dispensable for BIR dependent DNA synthesis at these replication-stressed chromosome ends.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the EdU-FISH data in double mutants.

claim: No changes in the frequency of telomere fragility were detected in TRF1-POLD3 nor TRF1-SMC5 mutants.
source: As previously reported, TRF1 depleted telomeres present approximately 20% of fragile telomeres per chromosomes (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, C). We could not detect any changes in the frequency of telomere fragility in TRF1-POLD3 nor TRF1-SMC5 mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, C) suggesting that neither POLD3 nor SMC5 are involved in the mechanism that gives rise to telomere fragility.
evidence: The claim is based on telomere fragility analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2, C.

claim: Neither POLD3 nor SMC5 are involved in the mechanism that gives rise to telomere fragility.
source: We could not detect any changes in the frequency of telomere fragility in TRF1-POLD3 nor TRF1-SMC5 mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 2, C) suggesting that neither POLD3 nor SMC5 are involved in the mechanism that gives rise to telomere fragility.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from telomere fragility data in double mutants.

claim: A significant reduction in number of cells having co-localising PML-telomere foci was detected in the double mutant cells TRF1-POLD3 and TRF1-SMC5.
source: As APBs were increased in TRF1 deleted cells (Figure 2C), we investigated the roles of POLD3 and SMC5 in the formation of these specialised bodies. A significant reduction in number of cells having co-localising PML-telomere foci was detected in the double mutant cells TRF1-POLD3 and TRF1-SMC5 (Figure 7A) suggesting that POLD3 and SMC5 are necessary for the formation of these recombination machinery loci.
evidence: The claim is based on APBs formation analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: POLD3 and SMC5 are necessary for the formation of APBs.
source: A significant reduction in number of cells having co-localising PML-telomere foci was detected in the double mutant cells TRF1-POLD3 and TRF1-SMC5 (Figure 7A) suggesting that POLD3 and SMC5 are necessary for the formation of these recombination machinery loci.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from APBs formation data in double mutants.

claim: Both types of T-SCE exchanges (single and double) are dependent on SMC5 and POLD3.
source: We next explored the involvement of these two factors in HR by scoring for T-SCE (Figure 7B), discriminating also between the two categories of T-SCEs (single or double exchanges) in the analysis of the double mutants TRF1-SMC5 and TRF1-POLD3. We found that both types of exchanges are dependent on SMC5 and POLD3 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is based on T-SCE analysis shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Only the absence of POLD3 was able to rescue the increase in TERRA levels detected in TRF1 deficient cells.
source: Finally, we assessed TERRA expression levels in the double mutants. Surprisingly, only the absence of POLD3 was able to rescue the increase in TERRA levels detected in TRF1 deficient cells, while the SMC5 single mutant increased TERRA expression (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA dot blot analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: The SMC5 single mutant increased TERRA expression.
source: Finally, we assessed TERRA expression levels in the double mutants. Surprisingly, only the absence of POLD3 was able to rescue the increase in TERRA levels detected in TRF1 deficient cells, while the SMC5 single mutant increased TERRA expression (Figure 7C).
evidence: The claim is based on RNA dot blot analysis shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Both POLD3 and SMC5 are essential for T-SCE and APBs formation.
source: Collectively, our data indicate that both POLD3 and SMC5 are essential for T-SCE and APBs formation, but only POLD3 is required to maintain increased TERRA levels and BIR observed in TRF1 deficient cells.
evidence: The claim is based on the collective interpretation of experimental data in double mutants.

claim: Only POLD3 is required to maintain increased TERRA levels and BIR observed in TRF1 deficient cells.
source: Collectively, our data indicate that both POLD3 and SMC5 are essential for T-SCE and APBs formation, but only POLD3 is required to maintain increased TERRA levels and BIR observed in TRF1 deficient cells.
evidence: The claim is based on the collective interpretation of experimental data in double mutants.

claim: POLD3 and SMC5 have separate roles or act at different stages of the recombination events happening at TRF1 depleted telomeres.
source: This suggests that POLD3 and SMC5 have separate roles or act at different stages of the recombination events happening at TRF1 depleted telomeres, advocating also an intriguing connection between TERRA and BIR.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the differential effects of POLD3 and SMC5 depletion.

claim: TERRA could trigger the homology search by stimulating the initial steps of BIR in which POLD3 is involved.
source: We speculate that TERRA could trigger the homology search by stimulating the initial steps of BIR in which POLD3 is involved (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the authors' interpretation of the data.

claim: Fragile sites are hotspots for deletions, chromosome rearrangements and are associated with an increased frequency of homologous recombination.
source: Fragile sites are hotspots for deletions, chromosome rearrangements and are associated with an increased frequency of homologous recombination (Glover and Stein, 1987).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Glover and Stein, 1987.

claim: Various factors suppress MTS and thereby facilitate DNA replication at telomeres, including the shelterin protein TRF1, the DNA helicases RTEL1, BLM and WRN, Topoisomerase TopoIIa and Rif1.
source: Various factors suppress MTS and thereby facilitate DNA replication at telomeres; including (Zaaijer et al., 2016) the shelterin protein TRF1 (Martínez et al., 2009; Sfeir et al., 2009), the DNA helicases RTEL1 (Vannier et al., 2012), BLM and WRN (Barefield and Karlseder, 2012), Topoisomerase TopoIIa (d'Alcontres et al., 2014) and Rif1 (Zaaijer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to published work.

claim: High levels of DNA damage and telomere fragility are characteristics of ALT cells.
source: High levels of DNA damage and telomere fragility are characteristics of ALT cells (Cesare et al., 2009) (Min et al., 2017), presenting several DNA repair and damage factors in APBs (Draskovic et al., 2009; Wu et al., 2000; Yeager et al., 1999), indication of elevated telomeric stress in these cells.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cesare et al., 2009 and Min et al., 2017.

claim: It has been hypothesized that ALT mechanism arises from persistent replication stress, which can be resolved by the initial collapse of the replication fork, subsequently offering substrates for HR repair mechanisms dependent on homology search and telomere synthesis as reported with BIR pathway.
source: Therefore, it has been hypothesized that ALT mechanism arises from persistent replication stress, which can be resolved by the initial collapse of the replication fork, subsequently offering substrates for HR repair mechanisms dependent on homology search and telomere synthesis as reported with BIR pathway (Dilley et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dilley et al., 2016.

claim: Replication stress generated at TRF1 depleted telomeres in telomerase positive MEFs is associated with the recruitment of ALT signature factors including PML, subunits of the NuRD complex, BRCA1 and SMC5/6 complex.
source: In this study, we report that replication stress generated at TRF1 depleted telomeres in telomerase positive MEFs is associated with the recruitment of ALT signature factors including PML, subunits of the NuRD complex, BRCA1 and SMC5/6 complex.
evidence: The claim is based on the PICh experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The formation of permissive telomeric chromatin enables transcription of telomeric sequences into TERRAs and increases recombination as measured by T-SCEs, in a POLD3 and SMC5/POLD3 dependent manner, respectively.
source: We suggest that the formation of permissive telomeric chromatin enables transcription of telomeric sequences into TERRAs and increases recombination as measured by T-SCEs, in a POLD3 and SMC5/POLD3 dependent manner, respectively.
evidence: The claim is based on the collective interpretation of experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Mitotic DNA synthesis is detected at TRF1 depleted telomeres, which is dependent on POLD3 but not SMC5.
source: Moreover, we detect mitotic DNA synthesis at TRF1 depleted telomeres, which is dependent on POLD3 but not SMC5.
evidence: The claim is based on EdU-FISH experimental data in double mutants.

claim: Comparison analysis with APH-treated MEFs highlighted the unappreciated role of mouse TRF1 in suppressing telomere chromatin re-organisation.
source: Comparison analysis with APH-treated MEFs highlighted the unappreciated role of mouse TRF1 in suppressing telomere chromatin re-organisation, which we propose to contribute to HR-dependent telomere-sister chromatid exchanges.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of experimental data between TRF1 deleted and APH-treated MEFs.

claim: Telomere replication stress induced by TRF1 deletion generates additional telomere responses (APBs, Chromatin remodeling, HR) compared to APH treated MEFs.
source: Herein, we showed that telomere replication stress induced by TRF1 deletion generates additional telomere responses (APBs, Chromatin remodeling, HR) compared to APH treated MEFs.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison of experimental data between TRF1 deleted and APH-treated MEFs.

claim: The difference in telomere responses between TRF1 deletion and APH treatment is imputed to the function of TRF1 in stabilising telomere chromatin.
source: We propose this is imputed to the function of TRF1 in stabilising telomere chromatin.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the comparison of experimental data.

claim: Mouse TRF1 is essential for cell proliferation and to counteract TERRAs expression/stability and activation of HR.
source: Mouse TRF1 is essential for cell proliferation and to counteract TERRAs expression/stability and activation of HR, while it seems dispensable in HT1080-ST and HeLa cells.
evidence: The claim is based on the collective interpretation of experimental data comparing mouse and human cells.

claim: TRF1 seems dispensable in HT1080-ST and HeLa cells.
source: Mouse TRF1 is essential for cell proliferation and to counteract TERRAs expression/stability and activation of HR, while it seems dispensable in HT1080-ST and HeLa cells.
evidence: The claim is based on the experimental data showing human cells can grow without TRF1.

claim: The difference between mouse and human TRF1 function could be explained by the difference in chromatin composition between the two species.
source: This could be explained by the difference in chromatin composition between the two species, indeed human telomeres display less abundant repressive marks compared to mouse chromosome ends (García-Cao et al., 2004; O'Sullivan et al., 2010; Rosenfeld et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is based on inference, with citations to García-Cao et al., 2004; O'Sullivan et al., 2010; Rosenfeld et al., 2009.

claim: Human telomeres display less abundant repressive marks compared to mouse chromosome ends.
source: This could be explained by the difference in chromatin composition between the two species, indeed human telomeres display less abundant repressive marks compared to mouse chromosome ends (García-Cao et al., 2004; O'Sullivan et al., 2010; Rosenfeld et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to García-Cao et al., 2004; O'Sullivan et al., 2010; Rosenfeld et al., 2009.

claim: Mouse and human TERRAs have different origins.
source: Moreover, mouse and human TERRAs have different origins.
evidence: The claim is a direct statement from the text.

claim: The main source of human TERRA molecules is from Human 20q subtelomere.
source: The main source of human TERRA molecules is from Human 20q subtelomere (Montero et al., 2016) however, other subtelomeres might contribute to local regulation and therefore control both cis and trans regulations (Tutton et al., 2016; Feretzaki et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Montero et al., 2016.

claim: Other subtelomeres might contribute to local regulation and therefore control both cis and trans regulations of human TERRAs.
source: The main source of human TERRA molecules is from Human 20q subtelomere (Montero et al., 2016) however, other subtelomeres might contribute to local regulation and therefore control both cis and trans regulations (Tutton et al., 2016; Feretzaki et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tutton et al., 2016; Feretzaki et al., 2019.

claim: Mouse TERRAs primary origin is controversial with reports proposing Chr18 subtelomere as the principal source in MEFs.
source: On the other hand, mouse TERRAs primary origin is more controversial with reports proposing Chr18 subtelomere as the principal source in MEFs (de Silanes et al., 2014), while recent literature hints to the subtelomeric regions of ChrX and ChrY (Chu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to de Silanes et al., 2014.

claim: Recent literature hints to the subtelomeric regions of ChrX and ChrY as the source of mouse TERRAs.
source: On the other hand, mouse TERRAs primary origin is more controversial with reports proposing Chr18 subtelomere as the principal source in MEFs (de Silanes et al., 2014), while recent literature hints to the subtelomeric regions of ChrX and ChrY (Chu et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Chu et al., 2017.

claim: PAR-TERRA would be more abundant and involved in trans regulation on the other chromosome ends.
source: These PAR-TERRA would be more abundant and involved in trans regulation on the other chromosome ends.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the cited literature about mouse TERRA origins.

claim: Telomere transcription appears to be differently regulated in human and mouse cells.
source: Telomere transcription appears to be differently regulated in human and mouse cells and it is tempting to speculate that the difference in chromatin composition between the two species is essential for different transcription regulations.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data comparing mouse and human cells.

claim: The difference in chromatin composition between mouse and human species is essential for different transcription regulations.
source: Telomere transcription appears to be differently regulated in human and mouse cells and it is tempting to speculate that the difference in chromatin composition between the two species is essential for different transcription regulations.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the authors' interpretation.

claim: It is plausible that human and mouse telomeres bear different accessibility to HR factors due to the distinct heterochromatin properties.
source: Therefore, it is plausible that human and mouse telomeres bear different accessibility to HR factors due to the distinct heterochromatin properties, that will undoubtedly be an interesting question to address in the future.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the authors' interpretation.

claim: Chromatin remodelling factors such as NuRD-ZNF827 are recruited to mouse TRF1 deficient telomeres to counteract the shelterin instability.
source: We suggest that chromatin remodelling factors such as NuRD-ZNF827 are recruited to mouse TRF1 deficient telomeres to counteract the shelterin instability.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the PICh data.

claim: In ALT telomeres, telomeric DNA sequence is interspersed with variant repeats, which are suggested to cause displacement of shelterin proteins.
source: This may be explained by analogy with ALT telomeres where telomeric DNA sequence is interspersed with variant repeats (Conomos et al., 2012; Marzec et al., 2015), which are suggested to cause displacement of shelterin proteins (Conomos et al., 2013), thus increasing replication stress and DDR.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Conomos et al., 2012; Marzec et al., 2015; Conomos et al., 2013.

claim: Nuclear receptors bind the interspersed variant repeats and recruit several chromatin remodelling factors including the NuRD complex, which can further alter the telomere architecture by increasing telomere compaction.
source: In this scenario, nuclear receptors bind the interspersed variant repeats and recruit several chromatin remodelling factors including the NuRD complex, which can further alter the telomere architecture by increasing telomere compaction (Conomos et al., 2014); perhaps a transient state before stimulating telomere associations and generating more 'open' recombination permissive conditions at telomeres.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Conomos et al., 2014.

claim: Repressive chromatin at DSBs has been proposed to facilitate homology search and promote recruitment of HR proteins like BRCA1.
source: In line with our findings, repressive chromatin at DSBs has been proposed to facilitate homology search and promote recruitment of HR proteins like BRCA1 (Khurana et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Khurana et al., 2014.

claim: The SMC5/6 complex plays the same role at replication induced telomeres as in ALT cells, targeting telomeres to PML bodies (APBs) and facilitating telomeric HR at these sites.
source: In addition to BRCA1, we have identified through PICh analysis the SMC5/6 complex specifically recruited at TRF1 deficient telomeres. We demonstrate that this complex plays the same role at replication induced telomeres as in ALT cells, targeting telomeres to PML bodies (APBs) and facilitating telomeric HR at these sites (Potts et al., 2006), since double mutant SMC5-TRF1 disrupts formation of APBs and reduces T-SCEs events.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data in double mutants, with a citation to Potts et al., 2006.

claim: TRF1 deficient MEFs do not display C-circles nor heterogeneity in telomere length and telomerase is still active.
source: However, we were unable to fully induce ALT in TRF1 deficient MEFs, as they display neither C-circles nor heterogeneity in telomere length and telomerase is still active.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplements 2.

claim: Telomerase could act as a stabiliser of telomeric DNA ends generated during fork restart.
source: The latter could act as a stabiliser of telomeric DNA ends generated during fork restart (Tong et al., 2015), similarly to what happens in RTEL1-/- MEFs (Margalef et al., 2018) and in human RTEL1 deficient cells with long telomeres (Porreca et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tong et al., 2015; Margalef et al., 2018; Porreca et al., 2018.

claim: Persistent DNA damage in ALT cells is suggested to originate from telomeric replication stress, which is proposed to be resolved by BIR in a POLD3 dependent manner.
source: Persistent DNA damage in ALT cells is suggested to originate from telomeric replication stress, which is proposed to be resolved by BIR in a POLD3 dependent manner (Dilley et al., 2016; Min et al., 2017; Roumelioti et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dilley et al., 2016; Min et al., 2017; Roumelioti et al., 2016.

claim: TRF1 is a major suppressor of telomeric replication stress and consequently of POLD3 dependent BIR.
source: Our results show that TRF1 is a major suppressor of telomeric replication stress and consequently of POLD3 dependent BIR.
evidence: The claim is based on the collective interpretation of experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TRF1 deficient telomeres present slower movement of S-phase replication forks, measured by molecular combing.
source: TRF1 deficient telomeres present slower movement of S-phase replication forks, measured by molecular combing (Sfeir et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Sfeir et al., 2009.

claim: The slower replication rates at telomeres is proposed to be a consequence of the hindrance of the replication forks by DNA secondary structures, including formation of G-quadruplexes on the lagging strand template or RNA-DNA hybrids.
source: The slower replication rates at telomeres is proposed to be a consequence of the hindrance of the replication forks by DNA secondary structures, including formation of G-quadruplexes on the lagging strand template or RNA-DNA hybrids.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the literature.

claim: In the absence of TRF1, BLM is unable to be recruited to replicated telomeres and to open DNA secondary structures.
source: In the absence of TRF1, BLM is unable to be recruited to replicated telomeres and to open DNA secondary structures (Lee et al., 2018; Zimmermann et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Lee et al., 2018; Zimmermann et al., 2014.

claim: In the absence of TRF1, POLD3 dependent BIR bypasses the stalled replication fork during G2/M phase.
source: Based on our results, we propose that in the absence of TRF1, POLD3 dependent BIR bypasses the stalled replication fork during G2/M phase.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Recent studies identified BIR as a mechanism to bypass RNA-DNA hybrids in a Rad52 and Pol32 dependent manner in yeast.
source: Recent studies identified BIR as a mechanism to bypass RNA-DNA hybrids in a Rad52 and Pol32 dependent manner in yeast (Amon and Koshland, 2016; Neil et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Amon and Koshland, 2016; Neil et al., 2018.

claim: POLD3 is necessary for the restart of stalled replication forks at RNA-DNA hybrids in human cells.
source: This mechanism is also conserved in human cells where POLD3 is necessary for the restart of stalled replication forks at RNA-DNA hybrids (Tumini et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tumini et al., 2016.

claim: Increased TERRAs levels at TRF1 depleted telomeres could form RNA-DNA hybrids that are bypassed by POLD3 dependent BIR.
source: Altogether, we propose that increased TERRAs levels at TRF1 depleted telomeres could form RNA-DNA hybrids that are bypassed by POLD3 dependent BIR (Figure 8).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data and model shown in Figure 8.

claim: TRF1 suppresses R-loop formation mediated by TRF2.
source: This is in agreement with recent findings showing that TRF1 suppresses R-loop formation mediated by TRF2 (Lee et al., 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Lee et al., 2018.

claim: SMC5 acts as inhibitor of TERRA accumulation, as its absence is causing a significant increase in TERRA levels.
source: In contrast to Pold3, SMC5 acts as inhibitor of TERRA accumulation, as its absence is causing a significant increase in TERRA levels.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Yeast Smc5 facilitates the resolution of toxic recombination intermediates at RNA-DNA hybrids generated by the helicase Mph1.
source: This result is reminiscent of the role of yeast Smc5 in facilitating the resolution of toxic recombination intermediates at RNA-DNA hybrids generated by the helicase Mph1 (Chen et al., 2009; Lafuente-Barquero et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2009; Lafuente-Barquero et al., 2017.

claim: SMC5 has a role in promoting T-SCEs, but not MiDAS formation, in the absence of TRF1.
source: We also describe a role of SMC5 in promoting T-SCEs, but not MiDAS formation (in contrast to PolD3), in the absence of TRF1.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data in double mutants.

claim: SMC5 has an exclusive function in HR at replicative-stressed telomeres, perhaps ensuring the right balance between accumulation and removal of HR-dependent intermediates formed during DNA repair.
source: These results are indicating an exclusive function of SMC5 in HR at replicative-stressed telomeres, perhaps ensuring the right balance between accumulation and removal of HR-dependent intermediates formed during DNA repair (Aragón, 2018).
evidence: The claim is based on inference from the experimental data, with a citation to Aragón, 2018.

claim: The lack of Smc5 in promoting MiDAS seems in apparent contradiction with a recent observation in ALT cells where telomeric MiDAS is decreased in SMC5/6-depleted Saos2 cells.
source: On the other hand, the lack of Smc5 in promoting MiDAS seems in apparent contradiction with a recent observation in ALT cells (Min et al., 2017), where telomeric MiDAS is decreased in SMC5/6-depleted Saos2 cells.
evidence: The claim is based on comparison with a citation to Min et al., 2017.

claim: The difference in SMC5 function in MiDAS is due to an imbalance of factors used for ALT maintenance, compared to the early events observed in the conditional system after only few population doublings.
source: We speculate, this difference is due to an imbalance of factors used for ALT maintenance, compared to the early events observed in our conditional system after only few population doublings.
evidence: The claim is speculative, based on the authors' interpretation.

claim: POLD3 and POLD4 subunits of the DNA polymerase delta are essential for CFS expression observed in human cells under replication stress.
source: Along with MUS81 structure specific nuclease, POLD3 and POLD4 subunits of the DNA polymerase delta are essential for CFS expression observed in human cells under replication stress (Minocherhomji et al., 2015; Tumini et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Minocherhomji et al., 2015; Tumini et al., 2016.

claim: TRF1-POLD3 double mutant did not show any suppression of telomere fragility.
source: To our surprise, TRF1-POLD3 double mutant did not show any suppression of telomere fragility, indicating key differences in the mechanism generating these phenotypes.
evidence: The claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2, C.

claim: TRF1 ensures telomeric chromatin stability and suppresses the recruitment of chromatin remodellers including NuRD and the formation of APBs, which together promote a HR prone environment.
source: In conclusion, our analysis of TRF1 function provides an unappreciated molecular understanding of the level of protection that this shelterin protein offers at telomeres. Surprisingly, we establish that TRF1 ensures telomeric chromatin stability and suppresses the recruitment of chromatin remodellers including NuRD and the formation of APBs, which together promote a HR prone environment.
evidence: The claim is based on the collective interpretation of experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: TRF1-dependent replication stress is associated with increased TERRAs expression/stability and activation of POLD3-dependent BIR to restart stalled/collapsed telomeric replication forks.
source: At the same time, TRF1-dependent replication stress is associated with increased TERRAs expression/stability and activation of POLD3-dependent BIR to restart stalled/collapsed telomeric replication forks.
evidence: The claim is based on the collective interpretation of experimental data presented in the manuscript.
